entries.829f140c1f6c29239b17f76142ef6eafd39163d0: <div sID="gen5718" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="1Sam.22" sID="1Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen5718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5719" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5720" type="x-p"/> David, being driven from Achish, returns into the land of Israel to be hunted by Saul. I. David sets up his standard in the cave of Adullam, entertains his relations (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1">ver. 1</reference>), enlists soldiers (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">ver. 2</reference>), but removes his aged parents to a more quiet settlement (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3-1Sam.22.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>), and has the prophet Gad for his counsellor, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">ver. 5</reference>. Saul resolves to pursue him and find him out, complains of his servants and Jonathan (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.6-1Sam.22.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), and, finding by Doeg's information that Ahimelech had been kind to David, he ordered him and all the priests that were with him, eighty-five in all, to be put to death, and all that belonged to them destroyed (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.19">ver. 9-19</reference>) from the barbarous execution of which sentence Abiathar escaped to David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20-1Sam.22.23">ver. 20-23</reference>.
entries.6d3bfff820958f124a738fbf2b40cedd91118f4f: <div eID="gen5720" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5719" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David in the Cave of Adullam. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5721" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they went down thither to him. <hi type="super">2</hi> And every one <hi type="italic">that was</hi> in distress, and every one that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in debt, and every one <hi type="italic">that was</hi> discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David went thence to Mizpeh of Moab: and he said unto the king of Moab, Let my father and my mother, I pray thee, come forth, <hi type="italic">and be</hi> with you, till I know what God will do for me. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he brought them before the king of Moab: and they dwelt with him all the while that David was in the hold. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the prophet Gad said unto David, Abide not in the hold; depart, and get thee into the land of Judah. Then David departed, and came into the forest of Hareth. <div eID="gen5721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5722" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David shelters himself in the cave of Adullam, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1">v. 1</reference>. Whether it was a natural or artificial fastness does not appear; it is probable that the access to it was so difficult that David thought himself able, with Goliath's sword, to keep it against all the forces of Saul, and therefore buried himself alive in it, while he was waiting to see (and he says here, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3">v. 3</reference>) what God would do with him. The promise of the kingdom implied a promise of preservation to it, and yet David used proper means for his own safety, otherwise he would have tempted God. He did not do any thing that aimed to destroy Saul, but only to secure himself. He that might have done great service to his country as a judge or general is here shut up in a cave, and thrown by as a vessel in which there was no pleasure. We must not think it strange if sometimes shining lights be thus eclipsed and hidden under a bushel. Perhaps the apostle refers to this instance of David, among others, when he speaks of some of the Old-Testament worthies that <hi type="italic">wandered in deserts, in dens and caves of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.38">Heb. xi. 38</reference>. It was at this time that David penned <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psalm cxlii.</reference>, which is entitled, <hi type="italic">A prayer when David was in the cave;</hi> and there he complains that <hi type="italic">no man would know him</hi> and that refuge failed him, but hopes that shortly the <hi type="italic">righteous would compass him about.</hi> <div eID="gen5722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5723" type="x-p"/> II. Thither his relations flocked to him, <hi type="italic">his brethren and all his father's house,</hi> to be protected by him, to give assistance to him, and to take their lot with him. <hi type="italic">A brother is born for adversity.</hi> Now, Joab, and Abishai, and the rest of his relations, came to him, to suffer and venture with him, in hopes shortly to be advanced with him; and they were so. The first three of his worthies were those that first owed him when he was in the cave, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15-1Chr.11.25">1 Chron. xi. 15</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen5723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5724" type="x-p"/> III. Here he began to raise forces in his own defence, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">v. 2</reference>. He found by the late experiments he had made that he could not save himself by flight, and therefore was necessitated to do it by force, wherein he never acted offensively, never offered any violence to his prince nor gave any disturbance to the peace of the kingdom, but only used his forces as a guard to his own person. But, whatever defence his soldiers were to him, they did him no great credit, for the regiment he had was made up not of great men, nor rich men, nor stout men, no, nor good men, but men <hi type="italic">in distress, in debt, and discontented,</hi> men of broken fortunes and restless spirits, that were put to their shifts, and knew not well what to do with themselves. When David had fixed his headquarters in the cave of Adullam, they came and enlisted themselves under him to the number of about 400. See what weak instruments God sometimes makes use of, by which to bring about his own purposes. The Son of David is ready to receive distressed souls, that will appoint him their captain and be commanded by him. <div eID="gen5724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5725" type="x-p"/> IV. He took care to settle his parents in a place of safety. No such place could he find in all the land of Israel while Saul was so bitterly enraged against him and all that belonged to him for his sake; he therefore goes with them to the king of Moab, and puts them under his protection, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3-1Sam.22.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Observe here, 1. With what a tender concern he provided for his aged parents. It was not fit they should be exposed either to the frights or to the fatigues which he must expect during his struggle with Saul (their age would by no means bear such exposure); therefore the first thing he does is to find them a quiet habitation, whatever became of himself. Let children learn from this to <hi type="italic">show pity at home and requite their parents</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1 Tim. v. 4</reference>), in every thing consulting their ease and satisfaction. Though ever so highly preferred, and ever so much employed, let them not forget their aged parents. 2. With what a humble faith he expects the issue of his present distresses: <hi type="italic">Till I know what God will do for me.</hi> He expresses his hopes very modestly, as one that had entirely cast himself upon God and committed his way to him, expecting a good issue, not from his own arts, or arms, or merits, but from what the wisdom, power, and goodness of God would do for him. Now David's father and mother forsook him, but God did not, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Ps. xxvii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen5725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5726" type="x-p"/> V. He had the advice and assistance of the prophet Gad, who probably was one of the sons of the prophets that were brought up under Samuel, and was by him recommended to David for his chaplain or spiritual guide. Being a prophet, he would pray for him and instruct him in the mind of God; and David, though he was himself a prophet, was glad of his assistance. He advised him to go into the land of Judah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">v. 5</reference>), as one that was confident of his own innocency, and was well assured of the divine protection, and was desirous, even in his present hard circumstances, to do some service to his tribe and country. Let him not be ashamed to own his own cause nor decline the succours that would be offered him. Animated by this word, there he determined to appear publicly. Thus are <hi type="italic">the steps of a good man ordered by the Lord.</hi>
entries.d5f1d2b41152536ea2a8091e60fcca90826a6380: <div eID="gen5726" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Destroys the Lord's Priests; the City of Nob Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> When Saul heard that David was discovered, and the men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, (now Saul abode in Gibeah under a tree in Ramah, having his spear in his hand, and all his servants <hi type="italic">were</hi> standing about him;) <hi type="super">7</hi> Then Saul said unto his servants that stood about him, Hear now, ye Benjamites; will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards, <hi type="italic">and</hi> make you all captains of thousands, and captains of hundreds; <hi type="super">8</hi> That all of you have conspired against me, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that sheweth me that my son hath made a league with the son of Jesse, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none of you that is sorry for me, or sheweth unto me that my son hath stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day? <hi type="super">9</hi> Then answered Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul, and said, I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he enquired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for him, and gave him victuals, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then the king sent to call Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Nob: and they came all of them to the king. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Saul said, Hear now, thou son of Ahitub. And he answered, Here I <hi type="italic">am,</hi> my lord. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Saul said unto him, Why have ye conspired against me, thou and the son of Jesse, in that thou hast given him bread, and a sword, and hast enquired of God for him, that he should rise against me, to lie in wait, as at this day? <hi type="super">14</hi> Then Ahimelech answered the king, and said, And who <hi type="italic">is so</hi> faithful among all thy servants as David, which is the king's son in law, and goeth at thy bidding, and is honourable in thine house? <hi type="super">15</hi> Did I then begin to enquire of God for him? be it far from me: let not the king impute <hi type="italic">any</hi> thing unto his servant, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> to all the house of my father: for thy servant knew nothing of all this, less or more. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the king said, Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech, thou, and all thy father's house. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; because their hand also <hi type="italic">is</hi> with David, and because they knew when he fled, and did not shew it to me. But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen, and asses, and sheep, with the edge of the sword. <div eID="gen5727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5728" type="x-p"/> We have seen the progress of David's troubles; now here we have the progress of Saul's wickedness. He seems to have laid aside the thoughts of all other business and to have devoted himself wholly to the pursuit of David. He heard at length, by the common fame of the country, that David <hi type="italic">was discovered</hi> (that is, that he appeared publicly and enlisted men into his service); and hereupon he called all his servants about him, and sat down under a tree, or grove, in the high place at Gibeah, with his spear in his hand for a sceptre, intimating the force by which he designed to rule, and the present temper of his spirit, or its distemper rather, which was to kill all that stood in his way. In this bloody court of inquisition, <div eID="gen5728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5729" type="x-p"/> I. Saul seeks for information against David and Jonathan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.7-1Sam.22.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Two things he was willing to suspect and desirous to see proved, that he might wreak his malice upon two of the best and most excellent men he had about him:—1. That his servant David did <hi type="italic">lie in wait</hi> for him and seek his life, which was utterly false. He really sought David's life, and therefore pretended that David sought his life, though he could not charge him with any overt act that gave the least shadow of suspicion. 2. That his son Jonathan stirred him up to do so, and was confederate with him in compassing and imagining the death of the king. This also was notoriously false. A league of friendship there was between David and Jonathan, but no conspiracy in any evil thing; none of the articles of their covenant carried any mischief to Saul. If Jonathan had agreed, after the death of Saul, to resign to David, in compliance with the revealed will of God, what harm would that do to Saul? Yet thus the best friends to their prince and country have often been odiously represented as enemies to both; even Christ himself was so. Saul took it for granted that Jonathan and David were in a plot against him, his crown and dignity, and was displeased with his servants that they did not give him information of it, supposing that they could not but know it; whereas really there was no such thing. See the nature of a jealous malice, and its pitiful arts to extort discoveries of things that are not. He looked upon all about him as his enemies because they did not say just as he said; and told them, (1.) That they were very unwise, and acted against the interest both of their tribe (for they were Benjamites, and David, if he were advanced, would bring the honour into Judah which was now in Benjamin) and of their families; for David would never be able to give them such rewards as he had for them, of <hi type="italic">fields and vineyards,</hi> and such preferments, to be colonels and captains. (2.) That they were unfaithful: <hi type="italic">You have conspired against me.</hi> What a continual agitation and torment are those in that give way to a spirit of jealousy! <hi type="italic">If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Prov. xxix. 12</reference>), that is, they seem to be so in his eyes. (3.) That they were very unkind. He thought to work upon their good nature with that word: <hi type="italic">There is none of you that is</hi> so much as <hi type="italic">sorry for me,</hi> or <hi type="italic">solicitous for me,</hi> as some read it. By these reasonings he stirred them up to act vigorously, as the instruments of his malice, that they might take away his suspicions of them. <div eID="gen5729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5730" type="x-p"/> II. Though he could not learn any thing from his servants against David or Jonathan, yet he got information from Doeg against Ahimelech the priest. <div eID="gen5730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5731" type="x-p"/> 1. An indictment is brought against Ahimelech by Doeg, and he himself is evidence against him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Perhaps Doeg, as bad as he was, would not have given this information if Saul had not extorted it, for had he been very forward to it he would have done it sooner: but now he thinks they must be all deemed traitors if none of them be accusers, and therefore tells Saul what kindness Ahimelech had shown to David, which he himself happened to be an eye-witness of. He had <hi type="italic">enquired of God for him</hi> (which the priest used not to do but for public persons and about public affairs) and he had furnished him with <hi type="italic">bread and a sword.</hi> All this was true; but it was not the whole truth. He ought to have told Saul further that David had made Ahimelech believe he was then going upon the king's business; so that what service he did to David, however it proved, was designed in honour to Saul, and this would have cleared Ahimelech, whom Saul had in his power, and would have thrown all the blame upon David, who was out of his reach. <div eID="gen5731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5732" type="x-p"/> 2. Ahimelech is seized, or summoned rather to appear before the king, and upon this indictment he is arraigned. The king sent for him and all the priests who then attended the sanctuary, whom he supposed to be aiding and abetting; and they, not being conscious of any guilt, and therefore not apprehensive of any danger, <hi type="italic">came all of them to the king</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.11">v. 11</reference>), and none of them attempted to make an escape, or to flee to David for shelter, as they would have done now that he had set up his standard if they had been as much in his interests as Saul suspected they were. Saul arraigns Ahimelech himself with the utmost disdain and indignation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear now, thou son of Ahitub;</hi> not so much as calling him by his name, much less giving him his title of distinction. By this it appears that he had cast off the fear of God, that he showed no respect at all to his priests, but took a pleasure in affronting them and insulting them. Ahimelech holds up his hand at the bar in those words: "<hi type="italic">Here I am, my lord,</hi> ready to hear my charge, knowing I have done no wrong." He does not object to the jurisdiction of Saul's court, nor insist upon an exemption as a priest, no, not though he is a high priest, to which office that of the judge, or chief magistrate, had not long since been annexed; but Saul having now the sovereignty vested in him, in things pertaining to the king, even the high priest sets himself on a level with common Israelites. <hi type="italic">Let every soul be subject</hi> (even clergymen) <hi type="italic">to the higher powers.</hi> <div eID="gen5732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5733" type="x-p"/> 3. His indictment is read to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.13">v. 13</reference>), that he, as a false traitor, had joined himself with the son of Jesse in a plot to depose and murder the king. "His design" (says Saul) "was to <hi type="italic">rise up against me,</hi> and thou didst assist him with victuals and arms." See what bad constructions the most innocent actions are liable to, how unsafe those are that live under a tyrannical government, and what reason we have to be thankful for the happy constitution and administration of the government we are under. <div eID="gen5733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5734" type="x-p"/> 4. To this indictment he pleads, Not guilty, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.14-1Sam.22.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. He owns the fact, but denies that he did it traitorously or maliciously, or with any design against the king. He pleads that he was so far from knowing of any quarrel between Saul and David that he really took David to have been then as much in favour at court as ever he had been. Observe, He does not plead that David had told him an untruth, and with that had imposed upon him, though really it was so, because he would not proclaim the weakness of so good a man, no, not for his own vindication, especially to Saul, who sought all occasions against him; but he insists upon the settled reputation David had as the most faithful of all the servants of Saul, the honour the king had put upon him in marrying his daughter to him, the use the king had often made of him, and the trust he had reposed on him: "He <hi type="italic">goes at thy bidding, and is honourable in thy house,</hi> and therefore any one would think it a meritorious piece of service to the crown to show him respect, so far from apprehending it to be a crime." He pleads that he had been wont to <hi type="italic">enquire of God for him</hi> when he was sent by Saul upon any expedition, and did it now as innocently as ever he had done it. He protests his abhorrence of the thought of being in a plot against the king: "<hi type="italic">Be it far from me.</hi> I mind my own business, and meddle not with state matters." He begs the king's favour: "<hi type="italic">Let him not impute</hi> any crime to us;" and concludes with a declaration of his innocency: <hi type="italic">Thy servant knew nothing of all this.</hi> Could any man plead with more evidences of sincerity? Had he been tried by a jury of honest Israelites, he would certainly have been acquitted, for who can find any fault in him? But, <div eID="gen5734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5735" type="x-p"/> 5. Saul himself gives judgment against him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech,</hi> as a rebel, <hi type="italic">thou and all thy father's house.</hi> What could be more unjust? <hi type="italic">I saw under the sun the place of judgment, that wickedness was there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Eccl. iii. 16</reference>. (1.) It was unjust that Saul should himself, himself alone, give judgment in his own cause, without any appeal to judge or prophet, to his privy council, or to a council of war. (2.) That so fair a plea should be overruled and rejected without any reason given, or any attempt to disprove the allegations of it, but purely with a high hand. (3.) That sentence should be passed so hastily and with so much precipitation, the judge taking no time himself to consider of it, nor allowing the prisoner any time to move in arrest of judgment. (4.) That the sentence should be passed not only on Ahimelech, himself, who was the only person accused by Doeg, but on <hi type="italic">all his father's house,</hi> against whom nothing was alleged: must the children be put to death for the fathers? (5.) That the sentence should be pronounced in passion, not for the support of justice, but for the gratification of his brutish rage. <div eID="gen5735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5736" type="x-p"/> 6. He issues out a warrant (a verbal warrant only) for the immediate execution of this bloody sentence. <div eID="gen5736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5737" type="x-p"/> (1.) He ordered his footmen to be the executioners of this sentence, but they refused, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.17">v. 17</reference>. Hereby he intended to put a further disgrace upon the priests; they may not die by the hands of the men of war (as <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.29">1 Kings ii. 29</reference>) or his usual ministers of justice, but his footmen must triumph over them, and wash their hands in their blood. [1.] Never was the command of a prince more barbarously given: <hi type="italic">Turn and slay the priests of the Lord.</hi> This is spoken with such an air of impiety as can scarcely be paralleled. Had he seemed to forget their sacred office or relation to God, and taken no notice of that, he would thereby have intimated some regret that men of that character should fall under his displeasure; but to call them <hi type="italic">the priests of the Lord,</hi> when he ordered his footmen to cut their throats, looked as if, upon that very account, he hated them. God having rejected him, and ordered another to be anointed in his room, he seems well pleased with this opportunity of being revenged on the priests of the Lord, since God himself was out of his reach. What wickedness will not the evil spirit hurry men to, when he gets the dominion! He alleged, in his order that which was utterly false and unproved to him, that they knew when David fled; whereas they knew nothing of the matter. But malice and murder are commonly supported with lies. [2.] Never was the command of a prince more honourably disobeyed. The footmen had more sense and grace than their master. Though they might expect to be turned out of their places, if not punished and put to death for their refusal, yet, come on them what would, they would not offer to fall upon the priests of the Lord, such a reverence had they for their office, and such a conviction of their innocence. <div eID="gen5737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5738" type="x-p"/> (2.) He ordered Doeg (the accuser) to be the executioner, and he obeyed. One would have thought that the footmen's refusal would awaken Saul's conscience, and that he would not insist upon the doing of a thing so barbarous as that his footmen startled at the thought of it. But his mind was blinded and his heart hardened, and, if they will not do it, the hands of the witness shall be upon the victims, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.7">Deut. xvii. 7</reference>. The most bloody tyrants have found out instruments of their cruelty as barbarous as themselves. Doeg is no sooner commanded to fall upon the priests than he does it willingly enough, and, meeting with no resistance, slays with his own hand (for aught that appears) on that same day eighty-five priests that were of the age of ministration, between twenty and fifty, for they <hi type="italic">wore a linen ephod</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.18">v. 18</reference>), and perhaps appeared at this time before Saul in their habits, and were slain in them. This (one would think) was enough to satiate the most blood-thirsty; but the horseleech of persecution still cries, "Give, give." Doeg, by Saul's order no doubt, having murdered the priests, went to their city Nob, and put all to the sword there (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">men, women, and children,</hi> and the cattle too. Barbarous cruelty, and such as one cannot think of without horror! Strange that ever it should enter into the heart of man to be so impious, so inhuman! We may see in this, [1.] The desperate wickedness of Saul when the Spirit of the Lord had departed from him. Nothing so vile but those may be hurried to it who have provoked God to give them up to their hearts' lusts. He that was so compassionate as to spare Agag and the cattle of the Amalekites, in disobedience to the command of God, could now, with unrelenting bowels, see the priests of the Lord murdered, and nothing spared of all that belonged to them. For that sin God left him to this. [2.] The accomplishment of the threatenings long since pronounced against the house of Eli; for Ahimelech and his family were descendants from him. Though Saul was unrighteous in doing this, yet God was righteous in permitting it. Now God performed against Eli that at which the ears of those that heard it must needs tingle, as he had told him that he would <hi type="italic">judge his house for ever</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.11-1Sam.3.13">ch. iii. 11-13</reference>. No word of God shall fall to the ground. [3.] This may be considered as a great judgment upon Israel, and the just punishment of their desiring a king before the time God intended them one. How deplorable was the state of religion at this time in Israel! Though the ark had long been in obscurity, yet it was some comfort to them that they had the altar, and priests to serve at it; but now to see their priests weltering in their own blood, and the heirs of the priesthood too, and the city of the priests made a desolation, so that the altar of God must needs be neglected for want of attendants, and this by the unjust and cruel order of their own king to satisfy his brutish rage—this could not but go to the heart of all pious Israelites, and make them wish a thousand times they had been satisfied with the government of Samuel and his sons. The worst enemies of their nation could not have done them a greater mischief.
entries.0737342660f6bbefa120cf01e6a0fdbe38ba562b: <div eID="gen5738" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abiathar's Escape. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5739" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Abiathar shewed David that Saul had slain the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's priests. <hi type="super">22</hi> And David said unto Abiathar, I knew <hi type="italic">it</hi> that day, when Doeg the Edomite <hi type="italic">was</hi> there, that he would surely tell Saul: I have occasioned <hi type="italic">the death</hi> of all the persons of thy father's house. <hi type="super">23</hi> Abide thou with me, fear not: for he that seeketh my life seeketh thy life: but with me thou <hi type="italic">shalt be</hi> in safeguard. <div eID="gen5739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5740" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The escape of Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, out of the desolations of the priests' city. Probably when his father went to appear, upon Saul's summons, he was left at home to attend the altar, by which means he escaped the first execution, and, before Doeg and his bloodhounds came to Nob, he had intelligence of the danger, and had time to shift for his own safety. And whither should he go but to David? <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20">v. 20</reference>. Let those that suffer for the Son of David <hi type="italic">commit the keeping of their souls to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1 Pet. iv. 19</reference>. 2. David's resentment of the melancholy tidings he brought. He gave David an account of the bloody work Saul had made among the priests of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.21">v. 21</reference>), as the disciples of John, when their master was beheaded, <hi type="italic">went and told Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.12">Matt. xiv. 12</reference>. And David greatly lamented the calamity itself, but especially his being accessory to it: <hi type="italic">I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.22">v. 22</reference>. Note, It is a great trouble to a good man to find himself in any way an occasion of the calamities of the church and ministry. David knew Doeg's character so well that he feared he would do some such mischief as this when he saw him at the sanctuary: <hi type="italic">I knew he would tell Saul.</hi> He calls him <hi type="italic">Doeg the Edomite,</hi> because he retained the heart of an Edomite, though, by embracing the profession of the Jewish religion, he had put on the mask of an Israelite. 3. The protection he granted to Abiathar. He perceived him to be terrified, as he had reason to be, and therefore bade him not to fear, he would be as careful for him as for himself: <hi type="italic">With me thou shalt be in safeguard,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.23">v. 23</reference>. David, having now time to recollect himself, speaks with assurance of his own safety, and promises that Abiathar shall have the full benefit of his protection. It is promised to the Son of David that God will <hi type="italic">hide him in the shadow of his hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>), and, with him, all that are his may be sure that they shall be in safeguard, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Ps. xci. 1</reference>. David had now not only a prophet, but a priest, a high-priest, with him, to whom he was a blessing and they to him, and both a happy omen of his success. Yet it appears (by <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">ch. xxviii. 6</reference>) that Saul had a high priest too, for he had a urim to consult: it is supposed that he preferred Ahitub the father of Zadok, of the family of Eleazar (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.8">1 Chron. vi. 8</reference>), for even those that hate the power of godliness yet will not be without the form. It must not be forgotten here that David at this time penned <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1-Ps.52.9">Psalm lii.</reference>, as appears by the title of that psalm, wherein he represents Doeg not only as malicious and spiteful, but as false and deceitful, because though what he said was, for the substance of it, true, yet he put false colours upon it, with a design to do mischief. Yet even then, when the priesthood had become as a withered branch, he looks upon himself as a <hi type="italic">green olive-tree in the house of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Ps. lii. 8</reference>. In this great hurry and distraction that David was continually in, yet he found both time and a heart for communion with God, and found comfort in it.  <chapter eID="1Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen5740" type="x-p"/>

entries.94b8be9ffd564b6b7ddcb093eaf97265e07881fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2734"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <div sID="gen3732" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1-1Sam.22.8">1Sa 22:1-8</reference>. David's Kindred and Others Resort to Him at Adullam.<div eID="gen3732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2734"/><hi type="bold">1. David ... escaped to the cave Adullam--</hi>supposed to be that now called Deir-Dubban, a number of pits or underground vaults, some nearly square, and all about fifteen or twenty feet deep, with perpendicular sides, in the soft limestone or chalky rocks. They are on the borders of the Philistine plain at the base of the Judea mountains, six miles southwest from Beth-lehem, and well adapted for concealing a number of refugees.<div eID="gen3733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his brethren and all his father's house ... went down--</hi>to escape the effects of Saul's rage, which seems to have extended to all David's family. From Beth-lehem to Deir-Dubban it is, indeed, a descent all the way. <div eID="gen3734" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d0336250318773d5c69be8f555a029518c1d584: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2735"/><div sID="gen3735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2735"/><hi type="bold">2. every one that was in distress--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Judg.11.3">Jud 11:3</reference>). <div eID="gen3735" type="x-p"/>
entries.33de010e2efc3b2a7ab98a1ad519cf08ae063fb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2736"/><div sID="gen3736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2736"/><hi type="bold">3. David went thence to Mizpeh of Moab--</hi>"Mizpeh" signifies a watchtower, and it is evident that it must be taken in this sense here, for it is called "the hold" or fort (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.4">1Sa 22:4</reference>). The king of Moab was an enemy of Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>), and the great-grandson of Ruth, of course, was related to the family of Jesse. David, therefore, had less anxiety in seeking an asylum within the dominions of this prince than those of Achish, because the Moabites had no grounds for entertaining vindictive feelings against him, and their enmity, to Saul rendered them the more willing to receive so illustrious a refugee from his court. <div eID="gen3736" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f69e06cbc14e587f10a3c822bff4491d476dcb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2737"/><div sID="gen3737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2737"/><hi type="bold">5. the prophet Gad said unto David, Abide not in the hold--</hi>This sound advice, no doubt, came from a higher source than Gad's own sagacity. It was right to appear publicly among the people of his own tribe, as one conscious of innocence and trusting in God; and it was expedient that, on the death of Saul, his friends might be encouraged to support his interest.<div eID="gen3737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest of Hareth--</hi>southwest of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen3738" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa37c6c6907242c7fd455731ba90510020557725: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2738"/><div sID="gen3739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2738"/><hi type="bold">6. Saul abode ... under a tree in Ramah--</hi>literally, "under a grove on a hill." Oriental princes frequently sit with their court under some shady canopy in the open air. A spear was the early scepter. <div eID="gen3739" type="x-p"/>
entries.54836aff9db2034b0152f951c64fd969d9124a4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2739"/><div sID="gen3740" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2739"/><hi type="bold">7-8. Hear now, ye Benjamites--</hi>This was an appeal to stimulate the patriotism or jealousy of his own tribe, from which he insinuated it was the design of David to transfer the kingdom to another. This address seems to have been made on hearing of David's return with his four hundred men to Judah. A dark suspicion had risen in the jealous mind of the king that Jonathan was aware of this movement, which he dreaded as a conspiracy against the crown.<div eID="gen3740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3741" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.16">1Sa 22:9-16</reference>. Doeg Accuses Ahimelech. <div eID="gen3741" type="x-p"/>
entries.1dc8b3d390bc500280b92f75100e8d33f7ff8af7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2740"/><div sID="gen3742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2740"/><hi type="bold">9. Doeg ... set over the servants--</hi>Septuagint, "the mules of Saul." <div eID="gen3742" type="x-p"/>
entries.33a4dfaee20abf55ffab27feb4d115eefb3a7d92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2741"/><div sID="gen3743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2741"/><hi type="bold">10. he inquired of the Lord for him--</hi>Some suppose that this was a malicious fiction of Doeg to curry favor with the king, but Ahimelech seems to acknowledge the fact. The poor simple-minded high priest knew nothing of the existing family feud between Saul and David. The informer, if he knew it, said nothing of the cunning artifice by which David obtained the aid of Ahimelech. The facts looked against him, and the whole priesthood along with him were declared abettors of conspiracy [1Sa 22:16, 17].<div eID="gen3743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3744" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.17-1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:17-19</reference>. Saul Commands to Kill the Priests. <div eID="gen3744" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e06008172dfc055255d13c37bb3c2407fd48806: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2742"/><div sID="gen3745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2742"/><hi type="bold">17-18. the footmen that stood about him--</hi>his bodyguard, or his runners (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.11">1Sa 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.1">2Sa 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.5">1Ki 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.28">1Ki 14:28</reference>), who held an important place at court (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.10">2Ch 12:10</reference>). But they chose rather to disobey the king than to offend God by imbruing their hands in the blood of his ministering servants. A foreigner alone (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.1-Ps.52.3">Psa 52:1-3</reference>) could be found willing to be the executioner of this bloody and sacrilegious sentence. Thus was the doom of the house of Eli fulfilled [1Sa 2:30-36]. <div eID="gen3745" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf187045377db84f8c80fa19163f70ab2290fce5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2743"/><div sID="gen3746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2743"/><hi type="bold">19. Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword--</hi>The barbarous atrocities perpetrated against this city seem to have been designed to terrify all the subjects of Saul from affording either aid or an asylum to David. But they proved ruinous to Saul's own interest, as they alienated the priesthood and disgusted all good men in the kingdom.<div eID="gen3746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3747" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20-1Sam.22.23">1Sa 22:20-23</reference>. Abiathar Escapes and Flees after David. <div eID="gen3747" type="x-p"/>
entries.932c9d7f2610b0ec7158ab6ede56ec7dcc32b365: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2744"/><div sID="gen3748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2744"/><hi type="bold">20-23. one of the sons of Ahimelech ... escaped--</hi>This was Abiathar, who repaired to David in the forest of Hareth, rescuing, with his own life, the high priest's vestments (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">9</reference>). On hearing his sad tale, David declared that he had dreaded such a fatal result from the malice and intriguing ambition of Doeg; and, accusing himself as having been the occasion of all the disaster to Abiathar's family, David invited him to remain, because, firmly trusting himself in the accomplishment of the divine promise, David could guarantee protection to him. <chapter eID="1Sam.22"/>

entries.a3d14869f94f1ac07747e3f390959124ab7c933a: <div eID="gen10331" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10332" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10333" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10333" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10332" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10334" type="x-p"/> David flees to the cave of Adullam, where he is joined by four hundred men of various descriptions, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1">1Sam 22:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1Sam 22:2</reference>. He goes afterwards to Moab; and by the advice of the prophet Gad, to the forest of Hareth, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3-1Sam.22.5">1Sam 22:3-5</reference>. Saul, suspecting his servants of infidelity, upbraids them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.6-1Sam.22.8">1Sam 22:6-8</reference>. Doeg informs him of David's coming to Nob; of his being entertained by Ahimelech; on which Saul slays Ahimelech and all the priests, to the number of eighty-five, and destroys the city of Nob, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.19">1Sam 22:9-19</reference>. Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, only escapes; he joins with David, by whom he is assured of protection, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20-1Sam.22.23">1Sam 22:20-23</reference>. <div eID="gen10334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10336" type="x-p"/> The cave Adullam - This was in the tribe of Judah, and, according to Eusebius and Jerome, ten miles eastward of what they call Eleutheropolis.
entries.0a0625c4bb2d9c9bcbc0b73cb421f2b8170a71b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10337" type="x-p"/> And every one that was in distress - debt - discontented - It is very possible that these several disaffected and exceptionable characters might at first have supposed that David, unjustly persecuted, would be glad to avail himself of their assistance that he might revenge himself upon Saul, and so they in the mean time might profit by plunder, etc. But if this were their design they were greatly disappointed, for David never made any improper use of them. They are never found plundering or murdering; on the contrary, they always appear under good discipline, and are only employed in services of a beneficent nature, and in defense of their country. Whatever they were before they came to David, we find that he succeeded in civilizing them, and making profitable to the state those who were before unprofitable. It is not necessary to strain the words of the original in order to prove that these were oppressed people, and not exceptionable characters, as some have done.
entries.cb06e9043fe14c1c844ffad4efa16e2ec54b2c10: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10338" type="x-p"/> He said unto the king of Moab - David could not trust his parents within the reach of Saul, and he found it very inconvenient to them to be obliged to go through all the fatigues of a military life, and therefore begs the king of Moab to give them shelter. The king of Moab, being one of Saul's enemies, would be the more ready to oblige a person from whom he might at least expect friendship, if not considerable services.
entries.d7e3944df7eeb886828763258cc8517c62dbcc16: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10339" type="x-p"/> Get thee into the land of Judah - Gad saw that in this place alone he could find safety.
entries.4ab83730e9a03446fc9156e1d256aa77a5995468: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10340" type="x-p"/> Saul abode in Gibeah - Saul and his men were in pursuit of David, and had here, as is the general custom in the East, encamped on a height, for so Ramah should be translated, as in the margin. His spear, the ensign of power (see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sam 18:11</reference> (note)), was at hand, that is stuck in the ground where he rested, which was the mark to the soldiers that there was their general's tent. <div eID="gen10340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10341" type="x-p"/> And all his servants were standing about him - That is, they were encamped around him, or perhaps here there is a reference to a sort of council of war called by Saul for the purpose of delivering the speech recorded in the following verses.
entries.909dad4f804a8b271b7ca3dc4e1b2a7b0df6c8cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10342" type="x-p"/> There is none that showeth me - He conjectured that Jonathan had made a league with David to dethrone him, and he accuses them of disloyalty for not making the discovery of this unnatural treason. Now it was impossible for any of them to show what did not exist, no such league having ever been made between David and Jonathan.
entries.222f2e305bbd4ebeae5fe3937baf85c2a8b881e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10343" type="x-p"/> Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul - In <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.7">1Sam 21:7</reference> he is said to be the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul, and the Septuagint intimate that he was over the mules of Saul. Probably he was what we call the king's equery or groom.
entries.b9aeceef8c90c6d5ad443621985c54ed3b30a4a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10344" type="x-p"/> And he inquired of the Lord for him - This circumstance is not related in history; but it is probably true, as David would most naturally wish to know where to direct his steps in this very important crisis.
entries.b5a36ee5490ee70f4f74f93cf9b2fbae912be649: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10345" type="x-p"/> And who is so faithful - The word נאמן neeman, which we here translate faithful, is probably the name of an officer. See the note on <reference osisRef="Num.12.7">Num 12:7</reference>.
entries.7390ff9eae1bf7990a4f113a3c690bec8510d424: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10346" type="x-p"/> Did I then begin to inquire of God - He probably means that his inquiring now for David was no new thing, having often done so before, and without ever being informed it was either wrong in itself, or displeasing to the king. Nor is it likely that Ahimelech knew of any disagreement between Saul and David. He knew him to be the king's son-in-law, and he treated him as such.
entries.d1b15802faa524b44af994395470738ddd6cc831: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10347" type="x-p"/> But the servants of the king would not - They dared to disobey the commands of the king in a case of such injustice, inhumanity, and irreligion.
entries.14efe26fe9a446d6fb9bfbd45d06c1f5f238b62d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10348" type="x-p"/> And Doeg - fell upon the priests - A ruthless Edomite, capable of any species of iniquity. <div eID="gen10348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10349" type="x-p"/> Fourscore and five persons - The Septuagint read τριακοσιους και πεντε ανδρας, three hundred and five men; and Josephus has three hundred and eighty-five men. Probably the eighty-five were priests; the three hundred, the families of the priests; three hundred and eighty-five being the whole population of Nob. <div eID="gen10349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10350" type="x-p"/> That did wear a linen ephod - That is, persons who did actually administer, or had a right to administer, in sacred things. The linen ephod was the ordinary clothing of the priests.
entries.0beaeb05bc6ec8c37d0dd4e789246c81b3ec2c31: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10351" type="x-p"/> And Nob - smote he with the edge of the sword - This is one of the worst acts in the life of Saul; his malice was implacable, and his wrath was cruel, and there is no motive of justice or policy by which such a barbarous act can be justified.
entries.e288abd435e82f39f6659b7f89843233057a86ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10352" type="x-p"/> Abiathar, escaped - This man carried with him his sacerdotal garments, as we find from <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sam 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">1Sam 23:9</reference>.
entries.83ab3ba83b8365c0eaaec21aa2d768c3bf5e8272: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen10352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10353" type="x-p"/> I knew it that day - When I saw Doeg there, I suspected he would make the matter known to Saul. <div eID="gen10353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10354" type="x-p"/> I have occasioned the death of all the persons - I have been the innocent cause of their destruction.
entries.e4058e564fc374ad658c70569872f12883146775: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen10354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10355" type="x-p"/> He that seeketh my life seeketh thy life - The enmity of Saul is directed against thee as well as against me, and thou canst have no safety but in being closely attached to me; and I will defend thee even at the risk of my own life. This he was bound in duty and conscience to do.  <chapter eID="1Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen10355" type="x-p"/>

entries.e9c7cfdad8b1d33759bcebb23feac5d065e85921: Having been driven away by Achish, the Philistian king at Gath, David took refuge in the cave Adullam, where his family joined him. The cave <hi type="italic">Adullam</hi> is not to be sought for in the neighbourhood of Bethlehem, as some have inferred from <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13-2Sam.23.14">2Sa 23:13-14</reference>, but near the town <hi type="italic">Adullam</hi>, which is classed in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference> among the towns in the lowlands of Judah, and at the foot of the mountains; though it has not yet been traced with any certainty, as the caves of <hi type="italic">Deir Dubban</hi>, of which Van de Velde speaks, are not the only large caves on the western slope of the mountains of Judah. When his brethren and his father’s house, i.e., the rest of his family, heard of his being there, they came down to him, evidently because they no longer felt themselves safe in Bethlehem from Saul’s revenge. The cave Adullam cannot have been more than three hours from Bethlehem, as Socoh and Jarmuth, which were near to Adullam, were only three hours and a half from Jerusalem (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.12.15">Jos 12:15</reference>).
entries.dfbc93ae8aba950bc55899bee2e88d1f4f7412e7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1Sa 22:2</reference> <div eID="gen4048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4049" type="x-p"/> There a large number of malcontents gathered together round David, viz., all who were in distress, and all who had creditors, and all who were embittered in spirit (bitter of soul), i.e., people who were dissatisfied with the general state of affairs or with the government of Saul, - about four hundred men, whose leader he became. David must in all probability have stayed there a considerable time. The number of those who went over to him soon amounted to six hundred men (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.13">1Sa 23:13</reference>), who were for the most part brave and reckless, and who ripened into heroic men under the command of David during his long flight. A list of the bravest of them is given in 1 Chron 12, with which compare 2Sa 23:13. and 1Ch 11:15.
entries.02bbb91b7aacfec99a4fa7f935734ce6a5565447: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3-1Sam.22.5">1Sa 22:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen4049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4050" type="x-p"/> David proceeded thence to <hi type="italic">Mizpeh</hi> in Moab, and placed his parents in safety with the king of the Moabites. His ancestress Ruth was a Moabitess. <hi type="italic">Mizpeh</hi>: literally a watch-tower or mountain height commanding a very extensive prospect. Here it is probably a proper name, belonging to a mountain fastness on the high land, which bounded the Arboth Moab on the eastern side of the Dead Sea, most likely on the mountains of Abarim or Pisgah (<reference osisRef="Deut.34.1">Deu 34:1</reference>), and which could easily be reached from the country round Bethlehem, by crossing the Jordan near the point where it entered the Dead Sea. As David came to the king of Moab, the Moabites had probably taken possession of the most southerly portion of the eastern lands of the Israelites; we may also infer this from the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, Saul had also made war upon Moab, for <hi type="italic">Mizpeh Moab</hi> is hardly to be sought for in the actual land of the Moabites, on the south side of the Arnon (Mojeb). אתּכם ... יצא־נא, “<hi type="italic">May my father and my mother go out with you</hi>.” The construction of יצא with את is a pregnant one: to go out of their home and stay with you (Moabites). “<hi type="italic">Till I know what God will do to me</hi>.” Being well assured of the justice of his cause, as contrasted with the insane persecutions of Saul, David confidently hoped that God would bring his flight to an end. His parents remained with the king of Moab as long as David was בּמּצוּדה, i.e., upon the mount height, or citadel. This can only refer to the place of refuge which David had found at Mizpeh Moab. For it is perfectly clear from <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">1Sa 22:5</reference>, where the prophet Gad calls upon David not to remain any longer בּמּצוּדה, but to return to the land of Judah, that the expression cannot refer either to the cave Adullam, or to any other place of refuge in the neighbourhood of Bethlehem. The prophet <hi type="italic">Gad</hi> had probably come to David from Samuel’s school of prophets; but whether he remained with David from that time forward to assist him with his counsel in his several undertakings, cannot be determined, on account of our want of information. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.9">1Ch 21:9</reference> he is called David’s seer. In the last year of David’s reign he announced to him the punishment which would fall upon him from God on account of his sin in numbering the people (2Sa 24:11.); and according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29">1Ch 29:29</reference> he also wrote the acts of David. In consequence of this admonition, David returned to Judah, and went into the wood <hi type="italic">Hareth</hi>, a woody region on the mountains of Judah, which is never mentioned again, and the situation of which is unknown. According to the counsels of God, David was not to seek for refuge outside the land; not only that he might not be estranged from his fatherland and the people of Israel, which would have been opposed to his calling to be the king of Israel, but also that he might learn to trust entirely in the Lord as his only refuge and fortress.
entries.6b391f88bfaa746223a47abb0ab390e61d382e64: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.6-1Sam.22.7">1Sa 22:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen4050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4051" type="x-p"/> Murder of the Priests by Saul. - 1Sa 22:6. When Saul heard that David and the men with him <hi type="italic">were known</hi>, i.e., that information had been received as to their abode or hiding-place, he said to his servants when they were gathered round him, “<hi type="italic">Hear</hi>,” etc. The words, “<hi type="italic">and Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk upon the height</hi>,” etc., show that what follows took place in a solemn conclave of all the servants of Saul, who were gathered round their king to deliberate upon the more important affairs of the kingdom. This sitting took place at Gibeah, the residence of Saul, and in the open air “<hi type="italic">under the tamarisk</hi>.” בּרמה, <hi type="italic">upon the height</hi>, not “under a grove at Ramah” (<hi type="italic">Luther</hi>); for <hi type="italic">Ramah</hi> is an appellative, and בּרמה, which belongs to האשׁל תּחת, is a more minute definition of the locality, which is indicated by the definite article (<hi type="italic">the</hi> tamarisk upon <hi type="italic">the</hi> height) as the well-known place where Saul’s deliberative assemblies were held. From the king’s address (“<hi type="italic">hear, ye Benjaminites; will the son of Jesse also give you all fields and vineyards?</hi>”) we perceive that Saul had chosen his immediate attendants form the members of his own tribe, and had rewarded their services right royally. גּם־לכלּכם is placed first for the sake of emphasis, “<hi type="italic">You Benjaminites also</hi>,” and not rather to Judahites, the members of his own tribe. The second לכלּכם (before ישׂים) is not a dative; but ל tub  merely serves to give greater prominence to the object which is placed at the head of the clause: <hi type="italic">As for all of you, will he make</hi> (you: see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §310, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.).
entries.bbdfb5df6ce6687464445a53b8d8d94d11ab85a3: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.8">1Sa 22:8</reference> <div eID="gen4051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4052" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">That you have all of you conspired against me, and no one informs me of it, since my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse</hi>.” בּכרת, lit. at the making of a covenant. Saul may possibly have heard something of the facts related in <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12-1Sam.20.17">1Sa 20:12-17</reference>; at the same time, his words may merely refer to Jonathan’s friendship with David, which was well known to him. ואין־חלה, “and no one of you is grieved on my account ... that my son has set my servant (David) as a lier in wait against me,” i.e., to plot against my life, and wrest the throne to himself. We may see from this, that Saul was carried by his suspicions very far beyond the actual facts. “As at this day:” cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.8.18">Deu 8:18</reference>, etc.
entries.8c20a13dbc6bd559ec1b258fb86a9ccd35b40359: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.10">1Sa 22:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen4052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4053" type="x-p"/> The Edomite Doeg could not refrain from yielding to this appeal, and telling Saul what he had seen when staying at Nob; namely, that Ahimelech had inquired of God for David, and given him food as well as Goliath’s sword. For the fact itself, see <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.10">1Sa 21:1-10</reference>, where there is no reference indeed to his inquiring of God; though it certainly took place, as Ahimelech (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.15">1Sa 22:15</reference>) does not disclaim it. Doeg is here designated נצּב, “<hi type="italic">the superintendent of Saul’s servants</hi>,” so that apparently he had been invested with the office of marshal of the court.
entries.e049ad9e043559c8af8515b224b4b4c9bcd4ad14: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.11-1Sam.22.15">1Sa 22:11-15</reference> <div eID="gen4053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4054" type="x-p"/> On receiving this information, Saul immediately summoned the priest Ahimelech and “<hi type="italic">all his father’s house</hi>,” i.e., the whole priesthood, to Nob, to answer for what they had done. To Saul’s appeal, “<hi type="italic">Why have ye conspired against me, thou and the son of Jesse, by giving him bread?</hi>” Ahimelech, who was not conscious of any such crime, since David had come to him with a false pretext, and the priest had probably but very little knowledge of what took place at court, replied both calmly and worthily (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.14">1Sa 22:14</reference>): “<hi type="italic">And who of all thy servants is so faithful</hi> (proved, attested, as in Num 12:7) <hi type="italic">as David, and son-in-law of the king, and having access to thy private audience, and honoured in thy house?</hi>” The true explanation of אל־משׁמעתּך סר may be gathered from a comparison of <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, where משׁמעת occurs again, as the context clearly shows, in the sense of a privy councillor of the king, who hears his personal revelations and converses with him about them, so that it corresponds to our “<hi type="italic">audience</hi>.” סוּר, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. to turn aside from the way, to go in to any one, or to look after anything (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.3">Exo 3:3</reference>; Rth 4:1, etc.); hence in the passage before us “<hi type="italic">to have access</hi>,” to be attached to a person. This is the explanation given by <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> and most of the modern expositors, whereas the early translators entirely misunderstood the passage, though they have given the meaning correctly enough at 2Sa 23:23. But if this was the relation in which David stood to Saul, - and he had really done so for a long time, - there was nothing wrong in what the high priest had done for him; but he had acted according to the best of his knowledge, and quite conscientiously as a faithful subject of the king. Ahimelech then added still further (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.15">1Sa 22:15</reference>): “<hi type="italic">Did I then begin to inquire of God for him this day?</hi>” i.e., was it the first time that I had obtained the decision of God for David concerning important enterprises, which he had to carry out in the service of the king? “<hi type="italic">Far be from me</hi>,” sc., any conspiracy against the king, like that of which I am accused. “<hi type="italic">Let not the king lay it as a burden upon thy servant, my whole father’s house</hi> (the omission of the <hi type="italic">cop</hi>. ו before בּכל־כּית may be accounted for from the excitement of the speaker); <hi type="italic">for thy servant knows not the least of all this</hi>.” בּכל־זאת, of all that Saul had charged him with.
entries.150b81874e60387c5f12ea71afb3d47cd2ff1f5d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.16-1Sam.22.17">1Sa 22:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen4054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4055" type="x-p"/> Notwithstanding this truthful assertion of his innocence, Saul pronounced sentence of death, not only upon the high priest, but upon all the priests at Nob, and commanded his רצים, “<hi type="italic">runner</hi>,” i.e., halberdiers, to put the priests to death, because, as he declared in his wrath, “<hi type="italic">their hand is with David</hi> (i.e., because they side with David), <hi type="italic">and because they knew that he fled and did not tell me</hi>.” Instead of the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> אזנו, it is probably more correct to read אזני, according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, although the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> may be accounted for if necessary from a sudden transition from a direct to an indirect form of address: “<hi type="italic">and</hi> (as he said) <hi type="italic">had not told him</hi>.” This sentence was so cruel, and so nearly bordering upon madness, that the halberdiers would not carry it out, but refused to lay hands upon “<hi type="italic">the priests of Jehovah</hi>.”
entries.52bf5da6826ddb5e9f9a7d729728548fb71295b2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.18">1Sa 22:18</reference> <div eID="gen4055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4056" type="x-p"/> Saul then commanded Doeg to cut down the priests, and he at once performed the bloody deed. On the expression “<hi type="italic">wearing the linen ephod</hi>,” compare the remarks at 1Sa 2:18. The allusion to the priestly clothing, like the repetition of the expression “<hi type="italic">priests of Jehovah</hi>,” serves to bring out into its true light the crime of the bloodthirsty Saul and his executioner Doeg. The very dress which the priests wore, as the consecrated servants of Jehovah, ought to have made them shrink from the commission of such a murder.
entries.74f16065c89675b1575b51ad23fa109df81e8a49: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:19</reference> <div eID="gen4056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4057" type="x-p"/> But not content with even this revenge, Saul had the whole city of Nob destroyed, like a city that was laid under the ban (vid., Deu 13:13.). So completely did Saul identify his private revenge with the cause of Jehovah, that he avenged a supposed conspiracy against his own person as treason against Jehovah the God-king.
entries.3b2d5b2e098c16dd6a3faf64eca1edd05d1d95f0: <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20-1Sam.22.23">1Sa 22:20-23</reference> <div eID="gen4057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4058" type="x-p"/> The only one of the whole body of priests who escaped this bloody death was a son of Ahimelech, named Abiathar, who “<hi type="italic">fled after David</hi>,” i.e., to David the fugitive, and informed him of the barbarous vengeance which Saul had taken upon the priests of the Lord. Then David recognised and confessed his guilt. “<hi type="italic">I knew that day that the Edomite Doeg was there, that he</hi> (i.e., that as the Edomite Doeg was there, he) <hi type="italic">would tell Saul: I am the cause of all the souls of thy father’s house</hi>,” i.e., of their death. סבב is used here in the sense of being the cause of a thing, which is one of the meanings of the verb in the Arabic and Talmudic (vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> <hi type="italic">Lex. s. v.</hi>). “<hi type="italic">Stay with me, fear not; for he who seeks my life seeks thy life: for thou art safe with me</hi>.” The abstract <hi type="italic">mishmereth</hi>, protection, keeping (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.6">Exo 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.16.33-Exod.16.34">Exo 16:33-34</reference>), is used for the concrete, in the sense of protected, well kept. The thought is the following: As no other is seeking thy life than Saul, who also wants to kill me, thou mayest stay with me without fear, as I am sure of divine protection. David spoke thus in the firm belief that the Lord would deliver him from his foe, and give him the kingdom. The action of Saul, which had just been reported to him, could only strengthen him in this belief, as it was a sign of the growing hardness of Saul, which must accelerate his destruction.  <chapter eID="1Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen4058" type="x-p"/>

                     </ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> none of you that is sorry for me, or shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth unto me, that my son hath stirred up my servant against me to lie in wait <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To design against my Crown, and Life, which will appear to be a most groundless suspicion, and false Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cusation.</ns0:note>, as at this day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 ¶ Then answered <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 52. title</ns0:note> Doeg the Edomite (which was set over the servants of Saul) and said, I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">See on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 21. 7.</ns0:note>, to Ahimelech the son of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 14. 3.</ns0:note> Ahitub.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And he enquired of the LORD for him <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">This is not Recorded, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 21. and therefore some think, that <ns0:hi>Doeg</ns0:hi> to curry-favour with <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> feigned this; for it is certain, <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> chargeth him with the Sin of Lying, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 52. 3. though it is not improbable, that he told other Lies also, not here expressed; and withal, he was guilty o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> concealing part of the Truth, which in this case he was ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liged to declare for <ns0:hi>Ahimelech</ns0:hi>'s just Defence; to wit, the cunning pretence and artifice whereby <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> circumvented <ns0:hi>Ahimeleth.</ns0:hi> Others think this was true, because <ns0:hi>Ahimelech</ns0:hi> seems to confess it, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15. though that may be spoken by way of concession. If it were so as <ns0:hi>Doeg</ns0:hi> declares, this was no new thing. Then he might add, that it was not so; though this be not here mentioned: for it is evident, That all his Answer or Apology, is not here expressed; for here is not a word of the Victuals or Sword which he gave him.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 21. 6, 9.</ns0:note> gave him victuals, and gave him the sword of Goliah the Philistine.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then the king sent to call Ahimelech the priest the son of Ahitub, and all his fathers house <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Of the House of <ns0:hi>Eli,</ns0:hi> which God had threatned to cut off, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 31.</ns0:note>, the priests that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> in Nob: and they came all of them to the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Saul said, Hear now, thou son of Ahi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tub <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He shews his Contempt and Anger, that he would not vouchsafe to Name him: See before, on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 20. 27.</ns0:note>: and he answered, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Hebr.</ns0:hi> behold me.</ns0:note> Here I <ns0:hi>am,</ns0:hi> my Lord.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And Saul said unto him, Why have ye con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spired against me, thou, and the son of Jesse, in that thou hast given him bread, and a sword, and hast enquired of God for him, that he should rise against me to lie in wait, as at this day?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 Then Ahimelech answered the king, and said, And who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> so faithful among all thy servants, as David <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He doth not determine the differences between <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>David;</ns0:hi> nor affirm, what <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> now was: but onely decla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red what <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had formerly been, both really, and in Pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lick Fame and Opinion.</ns0:note>, which is the kings son in law, and go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth at thy bidding, and is honourable in thine house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Did I then begin to enquire of God for him? be it far from me: let not the king impute <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> thing <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Or, this <ns0:hi>thing;</ns0:hi> to wit, which thou now chargest me with, That I should Assist <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in any evil Design against thee, or of thy suspition concerning him. For as for <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Attempts upon <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> well might <ns0:hi>Ahimelech</ns0:hi> impute them wholly to the violence of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Passion and Disease, seeing even <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> did so, as may be gathered from 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 2.</ns0:note> unto his servant, <ns0:hi>nor</ns0:hi> to all the house of my father: for thy servant knew nothing of all this <ns0:hi>e,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> little or great.</ns0:note> less or more.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And the king said, Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech, thou and all thy fathers house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 ¶ And the king said unto the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Guard.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> runners.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                     </ns0:gap>ootmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the LORD, because their hand <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with David, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they knew when he fled, and did not shew it me. But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the LORD <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Choosing rather to offend the King, by disobeying his wicked and bloody Command, than to offend God, by shed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding the Blood of such Innocent and Sacred Persons.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>go about,</ns0:hi> to wit, from man to man, till thou hast killed all.</ns0:note>, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mite <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Which is noted to wipe off the stain of this Butchery from the <ns0:hi>Israelitish</ns0:hi> Nation, and to shew, why he was so ready to do it, because he was one of that Nation which had an implacable hatred against all <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and against the Priests of the Lord.</ns0:note> turned, and he fell upon the priests, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2. 31.</ns0:note> slew on that day fourscore and five persons <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">With his own hand: which was not difficult, when no resistance was made.</ns0:note> that did wear a linnen ephod <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Not at that time, as some fancy, but usually such as used to Minister to the Lord in a linnen Ephod, which Priests and Levites used to do. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 28. 40. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And Nob the city of the priests smote he <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Doeg,</ns0:hi> with the help of some others whom <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> appointed to that work.                   <ns0:p n="20">20 ¶ And one of the sons of Ahimelech, the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Who by his Fathers death was now High-Priest.</ns0:note>, escaped and fled after David <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To <ns0:hi>Keilah, chap.</ns0:hi> 23. 6, 7.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And Abiathar shewed David, that Saul had slain the LORDS priests.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And David said unto Abiathar, I knew it <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">His malice and ambition made me suspect that he would do it.</ns0:note> that day, when Doeg the Edomite <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> there, that he would surely tell Saul: I have accasioned <ns0:hi>the death</ns0:hi> of all the persons of thy fathers house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Abide thou with me, fear not: for he that seeketh my life, seeketh thy life: but with me thou <ns0:hi>shalt be</ns0:hi> in safeguard <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Because God will certainly preserve me to the Kingdom which he hath promised: and I by his help will protect thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
